rules.title: Restricted or server-only secret is hardcoded in the app
rules.why: Anything in the app can be extracted by anyone who downloads it. A cloud key, model-provider key, payment key, repository token, or private key found this way lets an attacker spend your money or act as your servers.
rules.fix: Rotate the credential first, because it is already exposed. Then move the call behind your backend so the key never ships, and read server-side keys from your CI or server secret store.
rules.verify: Run `strings` on the release APK or IPA and search for the key's prefix; nothing should come back. Turn on push protection or a secret scanner so a new key can't be committed.

rules.title: Google API key in code (restrict it in the console)
rules.why: Maps and Firebase keys are client identifiers: they ship in every app and anyone can read them. Without restrictions, someone else can use your key and your quota.
rules.fix: In Google Cloud Console, restrict the key to your Android package name and signing certificate, or your iOS bundle ID, and to only the APIs it needs. If it calls a paid API such as Gemini, move that call behind your backend instead.
rules.verify: In Google Cloud Console, open the key's page and confirm it lists application restrictions and API restrictions.

rules.title: Client or API secret is assigned a literal value
rules.why: A value named as a secret ships inside the app, where anyone can extract it. An OAuth client secret in a mobile app protects nothing and lets others impersonate your app to the server.
rules.fix: Rotate the secret. Mobile OAuth clients should use PKCE with no client secret; other secrets belong on your backend. If the value is not a secret, rename it so reviewers can tell.
rules.verify: Search the release build with `strings` for the value; it should be gone.

rules.title: AES in ECB mode, or with no mode named
rules.why: ECB encrypts identical blocks to identical ciphertext, so patterns in the data show through, and it detects no tampering. On Android, `Cipher.getInstance("AES")` with no mode can silently give you ECB.
rules.fix: Use AES-GCM (`AES/GCM/NoPadding`) with a Keystore key, or Tink's AEAD, or CryptoKit's `AES.GCM` on iOS. Re-encrypt existing data under the new scheme.
rules.verify: Search for `AES/ECB`, `"AES"`, and `kCCOptionECBMode`; every remaining hit should be gone or explained in a comment.

fix_code.code:
import javax.crypto.Cipher
import javax.crypto.SecretKey
import javax.crypto.spec.GCMParameterSpec

private const val IV_BYTES = 12
private const val TAG_BITS = 128

fun encrypt(plaintext: ByteArray, key: SecretKey, aad: ByteArray): ByteArray {
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)          // the Keystore generates the IV; do not supply one
    cipher.updateAAD(aad)                          // e.g. "refresh_token", binds purpose to ciphertext
    val ciphertext = cipher.doFinal(plaintext)
    return cipher.iv + ciphertext                  // store the IV alongside; it is not secret
}

fun decrypt(stored: ByteArray, key: SecretKey, aad: ByteArray): ByteArray {
    val iv = stored.copyOfRange(0, IV_BYTES)
    val ciphertext = stored.copyOfRange(IV_BYTES, stored.size)
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, key, GCMParameterSpec(TAG_BITS, iv))
    cipher.updateAAD(aad)
    return cipher.doFinal(ciphertext)              // throws AEADBadTagException if tampered
}

rules.title: AES-CBC needs a separate MAC to detect tampering
rules.why: CBC hides data but doesn't detect changes. An attacker can alter ciphertext to change the plaintext predictably, and padding errors can leak the plaintext byte by byte.
rules.fix: Prefer AES-GCM. If you must keep CBC, compute an HMAC-SHA-256 over the IV and the ciphertext with a separate key, and check it in constant time before decrypting.
rules.verify: For each hit, confirm a MAC over IV plus ciphertext is checked before decryption, or that the code moved to GCM.

rules.title: Fixed IV or nonce
rules.why: An IV or nonce must be fresh for every message. With GCM, one repeat under the same key reveals the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker forge messages.
rules.fix: Don't supply an IV. Let the Keystore, Tink, or CryptoKit generate a random 12-byte nonce for each encryption, and store it next to the ciphertext.
rules.verify: For each encryption call, confirm the IV comes from `cipher.iv` after `init`, or from a secure random source, never from a constant.

import javax.crypto.Cipher
import javax.crypto.SecretKey

private const val IV_BYTES = 12

rules.title: MD5 or SHA-1 used to protect a password, signature, or token
rules.why: Attackers can build two different inputs with the same MD5 or SHA-1 hash, and both are fast to brute-force. Code that relies on them for passwords, signatures, or integrity can be forged or cracked.
rules.fix: Use SHA-256 or stronger. If the hash is only a non-security checksum, such as detecting a corrupted download, add a comment saying so.
rules.verify: For each hit, confirm it now uses SHA-256 or stronger, or a password hash such as Argon2id for passwords.

rules.title: Non-cryptographic or seeded random number generator
rules.why: Default random generators are built for speed, not unpredictability: an attacker can often predict later values from a few samples. A seeded generator repeats its values for anyone who can guess the seed.
rules.fix: For keys, nonces, salts, and tokens, use `SecureRandom()` with the default constructor on Android and `SecRandomCopyBytes` on iOS, and never seed them. Other uses, such as shuffling a list for display, are fine.
rules.verify: For each hit, confirm the value doesn't protect anything, or that it now comes from `SecureRandom` or `SecRandomCopyBytes`.

rules.title: Hardcoded plain-HTTP URL
rules.why: Anyone on the same network, such as public Wi-Fi, can read and change plain HTTP traffic. Even if the platform blocks cleartext today, an exception added later would let this URL through.
rules.fix: Change the URL to `https://`. If the server doesn't support HTTPS, fix the server; don't add a cleartext exception.
rules.verify: Build a release version and confirm requests to this host use HTTPS, or fail with a cleartext error.

rules.title: Token, password, or secret written to the log
rules.why: A token in a log line is a token on disk. Logs reach `adb logcat`, bug reports, and crash reporters that upload recent lines.
rules.fix: Remove the value from the message. Plant a release logging tree that drops everything below error, and strip `Log.v/d/i` with R8's `-assumenosideeffects`. On iOS, remove debug logging from release builds; where a log line stays, use `Logger` and leave dynamic values at the default `.private` privacy, never `privacy: .public` for a token.
rules.verify: Install a release build, sign in, and watch `adb logcat` (or Console.app on iOS): no token or password should appear.

rules.title: Encryption key is hardcoded in the app
rules.why: Anything in the app package is public. A key written in the code can be read from the APK or IPA in minutes, and then every copy of the encrypted data can be decrypted. It also can't be rotated without an app update.
rules.fix: Generate the key on the device inside the Android Keystore or the iOS Keychain or Secure Enclave, and never export it. Tink with a Keystore-protected keyset does this for you. If a server must decrypt, wrap a random per-session key with the server's public key instead of sharing one symmetric key.
rules.verify: For every `SecretKeySpec(`, `SymmetricKey(data:`, and `Key.from…(` call, confirm the key bytes come from the Keystore, the Keychain, Tink, or a secure random source, never from a string or byte literal.

rules.title: Secret copied to the clipboard without the sensitive flag
rules.why: Any app that reads the clipboard, and the keyboard, can see a copied password, code, or token. Android 13 and later show the copied text in a preview unless the clip is marked sensitive.
rules.fix: Don't copy secrets. If the user asks to copy one, set `ClipDescription.EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE` in the clip's extras (API 33+) and clear the clip after a short timeout.
rules.verify: Copy the value on an Android 13 device and confirm the system preview shows dots instead of the text.

rules.title: Broken cipher (DES, 3DES, RC4, RC2, or Blowfish)
rules.why: DES keys can be brute-forced, 3DES and Blowfish use 64-bit blocks that leak data after a few gigabytes (Sweet32), and RC4's output is biased. Data encrypted with them should be treated as readable.
rules.fix: Use AES-GCM through the Keystore, CryptoKit, or Tink. Re-encrypt stored legacy data with the new scheme the first time you read it.
rules.verify: Search for `DES`, `RC4`, `RC2`, `Blowfish`, and `kCCAlgorithm`; only AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 should remain.

fix_code.code:
val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, keystoreKey)          // the Keystore picks a random IV
val stored = cipher.iv + cipher.doFinal(plaintext)

rules.title: Encryption key is too small
rules.why: RSA, DSA, and DH keys below 2,048 bits, curves below 224 bits, and symmetric keys below 128 bits can be broken with today's hardware, which exposes everything they protect or sign.
rules.fix: Use P-256 (EC) keys generated in the Keystore or Secure Enclave. If you need RSA, use at least 2,048 bits, and 3,072 for keys that must last beyond 2030.
rules.verify: For each key generator, confirm the size is at least 2,048 bits for RSA, a curve of at least P-256, or at least 128 bits for AES.

rules.title: PBKDF2 uses too few iterations
rules.why: A password-derived key is only as strong as the work an attacker must repeat per guess. With few PBKDF2 iterations, a stolen salt and hash or ciphertext falls to a GPU dictionary attack in hours.
rules.fix: Prefer Argon2id. If PBKDF2 is required, use HMAC-SHA-256 with at least 600,000 iterations. For a short PIN, gate a Keystore or Secure Enclave key with user authentication instead.
rules.verify: Confirm the iteration count meets OWASP's minimum for the PRF: 600,000 for HMAC-SHA-256, 210,000 for HMAC-SHA-512, 1,300,000 for HMAC-SHA-1.

fix_code.code:
val spec = PBEKeySpec(password, salt, 600_000, 256)   // salt: 16 random bytes per secret
val key = SecretKeyFactory.getInstance("PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256").generateSecret(spec)
spec.clearPassword()

rules.title: Password hashing uses a fixed salt
rules.why: A salt written in the code is the same for every user and install, so one precomputed table or one GPU run attacks every derived key at once, and equal passwords give equal keys.
rules.fix: Generate a random 16-byte salt per secret with `SecureRandom` or `SecRandomCopyBytes`, and store it next to the derived data.
rules.verify: For each PBKDF2 call, confirm the salt comes from a secure random source or from storage, never from a literal.

rules.title: gRPC channel sends traffic in plain text
rules.why: A plaintext gRPC channel skips TLS entirely, and Network Security Config and ATS don't cover gRPC sockets. Anyone on the network can read and change every call, including auth metadata.
rules.fix: Use `useTransportSecurity()` (grpc-java), `.tls` (grpc-swift), or `ChannelCredentials.secure()` (grpc-dart). Keep plaintext only for a local test server in debug builds.
rules.verify: Capture the app's gRPC traffic with a proxy and confirm it is a TLS handshake, not readable HTTP/2 frames.

rules.title: Biometric check falls back to the device passcode
rules.why: When the prompt also accepts the device PIN or passcode, anyone who has watched the user unlock the phone can approve the action. For a payment or a vault unlock, that removes the point of the biometric.
rules.fix: For high-value actions, require `BIOMETRIC_STRONG` or `.biometryCurrentSet` with a key bound to it. Make the fallback a server-side step-up (password, passkey, or OTP), not the device PIN.
rules.verify: Trigger the sensitive action and confirm the prompt offers no "Use PIN" or "Enter Passcode" option.
rules.not_needed_reason: A device-passcode fallback is fine for unlocking an app that holds no high-value data.

rules.title: Private key or client certificate ships inside the app
rules.why: Anything in the app package is public. A bundled private key, or a client-certificate keystore with its password in the code, lets anyone impersonate the app to your mTLS server or sign as you.
rules.fix: Remove the key and rotate it. For mTLS, have each device generate its key pair in the Keystore or Secure Enclave and enroll it with your server.
rules.verify: Unpack the release APK or IPA and search it for `PRIVATE KEY` and for `.p12`, `.pfx`, `.pem`, and `.key` files; nothing should be found.

rules.title: Zip entry name is used as a path without a containment check (Zip Slip)
rules.why: An archive entry named `../../shared_prefs/x.xml` writes outside the folder you meant. A malicious download or a shared file can then overwrite app code, preferences, or databases.
rules.fix: Resolve the canonical path of each output file and reject the entry unless it starts with the target folder's canonical path plus a separator.
rules.verify: Extract an archive whose entry is named `../evil.txt` and confirm the app refuses it and nothing is written outside the target folder.

rules.title: No root or jailbreak detection found
rules.why: A rooted or jailbroken device lets other code read the app's memory and storage and hook its checks. Without any signal, your backend can't weigh that risk for a payment or sign-in.
rules.fix: Collect root and jailbreak signals, or better, attestation (Play Integrity, App Attest), and send them to the backend as risk signals. Report; don't block locally. In React Native, jail-monkey gives root and jailbreak signals, and @react-native-firebase/app-check or react-native-device-attest gives attestation.
rules.verify: Run the app on a rooted emulator or a jailbroken device and confirm the backend receives the signal.

rules.title: No debugger detection found
rules.why: An attached debugger can read keys from memory and skip any client-side check. Without a debugger signal, the backend can't tell a tampered session from a normal one.
rules.fix: Add JDWP and TracerPid checks on Android, and the `sysctl` P_TRACED check on iOS, to the signals you report, and run them during sensitive flows, not only at startup. In React Native, freerasp-react-native reports debugger, emulator, and hooking signals.
rules.verify: Attach a debugger to a release build and confirm the signal reaches the backend.

rules.title: RSA encryption uses PKCS #1 v1.5 or no padding
rules.why: PKCS #1 v1.5 encryption padding is open to padding-oracle attacks that recover the plaintext, and raw RSA with no padding is deterministic and malleable. `Cipher.getInstance("RSA")` picks PKCS #1 v1.5.
rules.fix: Use `RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-256AndMGF1Padding` (on the Keystore, set the MGF1 digest to SHA-1), or better, ECDH with AES-GCM.
rules.verify: Search for `"RSA"`, `PKCS1Padding`, `NoPadding`, and `rsaEncryptionPKCS1`; only OAEP should remain.

rules.title: Signature uses SHA-1 or MD5
rules.why: A signature over a SHA-1 or MD5 hash can be forged by finding a colliding message. Anything that trusts the signature, such as a license, an update, or a request, can then be faked.
rules.fix: Sign with SHA-256 or stronger, for example `SHA256withECDSA` on a P-256 key.
rules.verify: Search for `SHA1with`, `MD5with`, `NONEwith`, and `SHA1` signature algorithms; none should remain.

rules.title: MAC or signature compared with an ordinary equality check
rules.why: `Arrays.equals`, `contentEquals`, and `==` stop at the first byte that differs, so response time reveals how much of a guessed MAC is right. An attacker can then forge a valid tag byte by byte.
rules.fix: Compare MACs with `MessageDigest.isEqual` on the JVM, `HMAC.isValidAuthenticationCode` in CryptoKit, or a constant-time compare in Dart.
rules.verify: For each MAC or signature check, confirm it uses a constant-time comparison.

rules.title: Generated key is saved next to the data it protects
rules.why: A key generated in app memory and written to preferences or a file sits beside its ciphertext. Anyone who can copy the app's storage, from a backup or a rooted device, gets both.
rules.fix: Generate the key inside the Android Keystore or the Secure Enclave, or use Tink with an `android-keystore://` master key, so the raw key never reaches storage.
rules.verify: For each generated key, confirm its bytes are never written to preferences, DataStore, UserDefaults, or a file, unless wrapped by a Keystore or Keychain key.

rules.title: SecRandomCopyBytes result is not checked
rules.why: `SecRandomCopyBytes` reports failure through its return status. If it fails and the status is ignored, the buffer keeps its initial zeros and becomes a predictable key, nonce, or salt.
rules.fix: Check the status: `guard status == errSecSuccess else { throw … }`. For keys, `SymmetricKey(size:)` handles this for you.
rules.verify: Search for `SecRandomCopyBytes` and confirm every call's return value is compared with `errSecSuccess`.

rules.title: App never checks that the device has a screen lock
rules.why: On a device with no PIN, pattern, or passcode, the Keystore and Keychain protect nothing from someone holding the phone. Without a check, the app can't warn the user or bind secrets to the lock.
rules.fix: Bind secrets to keys that need a screen lock (`setUserAuthenticationRequired`, `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly`), and check `isDeviceSecure` or `canEvaluatePolicy`.
rules.verify: Remove the screen lock on a test device and confirm the app warns the user or refuses the sensitive feature.

rules.title: App code writes a secret into the WebView's DOM
rules.why: Once a code, token, or balance is in the page's DOM, every script on the page can read it, including third-party or injected scripts. The native side has no control over it afterward.
rules.fix: Render the value in a native view over the WebView, or pass it through a narrow, origin-checked message channel that never writes it into the DOM.
rules.verify: Inspect the WebView with remote debugging on a debug build and confirm the secret never appears in the DOM.

rules.title: Embedded TLS library skips certificate checks or allows old TLS
rules.why: libcurl, OpenSSL, BoringSSL, wolfSSL, and mbedTLS bypass the platform's TLS settings. With verification off, anyone on the network can impersonate the server; below TLS 1.2, old protocol attacks apply.
rules.fix: Verify the peer and the host name (`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER` and `VERIFYHOST` on, `SSL_VERIFY_PEER`), and set TLS 1.2 as the minimum version.
rules.verify: Send the native traffic through a proxy whose CA the device doesn't trust and confirm the handshake fails.

rules.title: Local database stores credentials without encryption
rules.why: Room, raw SQLite, Realm, Core Data, and Hive write plain files in the app sandbox. They reach backups and anyone with file access, so a token or password column there can be lifted and replayed.
rules.fix: Keep tokens out of the database, or encrypt it: SQLCipher through `SupportOpenHelperFactory` with a Keystore-wrapped passphrase, Realm's `encryptionKey`, Hive's `encryptionCipher`, or on iOS a file protection class (`NSPersistentStoreFileProtectionKey`).
rules.verify: Pull the database file from a test device and open it with `sqlite3`; no token or password should be readable.

rules.title: Notification shows a one-time code or a balance on the lock screen
rules.why: Lock-screen notifications are readable by anyone holding the phone. A one-time code there lets a thief finish a sign-in or a transfer without unlocking the device.
rules.fix: Set `VISIBILITY_PRIVATE` with a redacted `setPublicVersion` on Android. On iOS, send a generic message and fetch the detail after unlock.
rules.verify: Trigger the notification with the phone locked and confirm the code or balance is hidden.

rules.title: Password or PIN field shows the typed text
rules.why: An unmasked password or PIN field shows the secret to anyone looking at the screen and to screen recording, and the keyboard may learn and suggest it later.
rules.fix: Use a password input type (`textPassword`, `numberPassword`), `PasswordVisualTransformation`, `SecureField`, `isSecureTextEntry = true`, or `obscureText: true`. A show-password toggle is fine.
rules.verify: Type into the field and confirm the characters are masked, and that the keyboard offers no suggestions.

rules.title: Analytics SDK receives personal data
rules.why: Email addresses and phone numbers sent to analytics or crash SDKs leave your control, end up in third-party dashboards, and must be declared in Data safety and privacy labels.
rules.fix: Send a pseudonymous ID instead, and keep personal data out of event parameters and custom keys.
rules.verify: Capture the SDK's traffic or check its dashboard and confirm no email, phone number, or name appears.

rules.title: Native code is built without compiler protections
rules.why: Stack canaries, position-independent code, RELRO, FORTIFY_SOURCE, and ARC are free defaults that make memory-corruption bugs much harder to exploit. These flags turn them off.
rules.fix: Remove the flags; the toolchain defaults are safe. Migrate files compiled with `-fno-objc-arc` to ARC.
rules.verify: Check the release binary: `checksec` or `readelf` on the `.so`, `otool -hv` and `otool -Iv` on the Mach-O, should show PIE, canaries, and RELRO.

rules.title: Staging, test, or private-network endpoint in release code
rules.why: A staging or development host in the release build points attackers at systems that are usually less protected, and a private address or the emulator's host address means debug wiring shipped.
rules.fix: Inject endpoints per build type or flavor, and keep non-production hosts out of the release variant.
rules.verify: Unpack the release build and search its strings for `staging`, `dev.`, `10.0.2.2`, and private addresses; none should remain.

rules.title: OAuth sign-in uses a flow RFC 8252 rules out
rules.why: The implicit flow puts tokens in a redirect any app can intercept, the password grant hands the user's password to the app, `plain` PKCE adds no protection, and a WebView sign-in page lets the app read the password.
rules.fix: Use the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256) in Custom Tabs, Auth Tab, or `ASWebAuthenticationSession`, for example through AppAuth.
rules.verify: Sign in and confirm the browser, not a WebView, shows the login page, and that the request carries `response_type=code` and `code_challenge_method=S256`.

fix_code.code:
val request = AuthorizationRequest.Builder(
    serviceConfig, clientId, ResponseTypeValues.CODE, redirectUri,
).setScope("openid profile").build()     // AppAuth adds PKCE S256 by default
startActivityForResult(authService.getAuthorizationRequestIntent(request), RC_AUTH)

rules.title: No emulator detection found
rules.why: Fraud and cheating at scale run on emulators. Without an emulator signal, the backend can't tell a farm of virtual devices from real users.
rules.fix: Add emulator signals (build fingerprint, hardware, `ro.kernel.qemu`; the iOS simulator environment) to the set you report, and rely on attestation for the strong signal. In React Native, freerasp-react-native reports these signals.
rules.verify: Run a release build on an emulator and confirm the signal reaches the backend.

rules.title: No hooking or instrumentation detection found
rules.why: Frida, Xposed, and Substrate rewrite the app's checks at runtime. Without a hooking signal, the backend trusts results that the attacker computed.
rules.fix: Add Frida and Xposed signals (ports, loaded libraries, `/proc/self/maps`) to the set you report, and rely on attestation for the strong signal. In React Native, freerasp-react-native reports these signals.
rules.verify: Attach Frida to a release build and confirm the signal reaches the backend.

rules.title: App has no way to force an update
rules.why: When a security bug ships, users on the old version stay exposed until they update. Without a forced update path, you can't retire a vulnerable version.
rules.fix: Keep a server-side minimum version and enforce it with Play's in-app updates (`IMMEDIATE`) or an App Store redirect.
rules.verify: Raise the minimum version on the server and confirm an older build blocks sensitive features until the user updates.

rules.title: Jackson accepts attacker-chosen classes
rules.why: Default typing and `JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS` let the JSON name the class to build. With a gadget class on the classpath, crafted input becomes code execution or file access.
rules.fix: Use `JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME` with registered subtypes, or kotlinx.serialization with sealed classes.
rules.verify: Search for `enableDefaultTyping`, `activateDefaultTyping`, and `Id.CLASS`; none should remain.

rules.title: Shell command built from a variable
rules.why: A command string with input in it lets that input add its own commands. On a phone, that runs with the app's identity and reaches its files and keys.
rules.fix: Don't run shell commands with input. If you must start a process, pass a fixed program and an argument array, and validate each argument.
rules.verify: For each process call, confirm the program is a constant and no argument comes from input.

rules.title: Password, PIN, or username is checked against a value in the code
rules.why: A login, PIN, or developer backdoor that compares input with a fixed string ships that string in the app. Anyone who unpacks the app can read it and pass the check.
rules.fix: Check credentials on your server, never against a value in the app. Remove developer or debug accounts from release builds.
rules.verify: Search the release build with `strings` for the value; it should be gone, and the login should fail without the server.

rules.title: Password or token is written to a file in plain text
rules.why: A file, plist, cookie, or document store in the app's folder is readable on a rooted or jailbroken device and is copied into backups. A password or token there can be lifted and reused.
rules.fix: Keep credentials in the Android Keystore or the iOS Keychain. If a file must hold one, encrypt it with a Keystore- or Keychain-protected key, and better still, don't store it at all.
rules.verify: Pull the app's data folder from a test device and search it for the password or token; it should not appear.

rules.title: Token, nonce, or random value is taken from the clock
rules.why: The current time is known to anyone within a few seconds. A token, nonce, or one-time code made from it can be guessed by trying the times around when it was made.
rules.fix: Use `SecureRandom` on Android, `SecRandomCopyBytes` or `SystemRandomNumberGenerator` on iOS, and `Random.secure()` in Dart. Keep timestamps for expiry only.
rules.verify: Make two values a millisecond apart; they should share no visible pattern.

rules.title: Web page or HTML string inserts untrusted text as markup
rules.why: Text from the page's URL, or typed by the user, becomes HTML. A crafted link or entry can then add a script that runs inside your WebView, with access to its data and any JavaScript bridge.
rules.fix: Set `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`, or escape the value before you add it to HTML. Don't build `loadHTMLString` or `loadDataWithBaseURL` content from input.
rules.verify: Enter `` as the value; it should show as text, and no alert should appear.

rules.title: Native code copies Java input into a fixed buffer without a length check
rules.why: `strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf`, and `gets` copy until the input ends. A string from Java that is longer than the buffer overwrites memory next to it, which can crash the app or run code.
rules.fix: Use `strlcpy`, `strlcat`, or `snprintf` with the buffer size, and check the length of the input against the buffer before you copy.
rules.verify: Pass a string longer than the buffer from Java; the app should reject it or truncate it without crashing.

rules.title: App reads sensitive page data in the page's JavaScript world
rules.why: `evaluateJavaScript` without a content world runs in the page's own world. A script on the page can replace `document.querySelector` first, so the app reads an account number or amount the attacker chose.
rules.fix: Run app scripts in `.defaultClient` or a named `WKContentWorld` with `evaluateJavaScript(_:in:in:completionHandler:)` (iOS 14 or later).
rules.verify: Override `document.querySelector` from the page, then trigger the read; the app should still get the real value.
